q: What does Sec. 4.4.1 recommend regarding the use of a single method of compensation across an entire project?
o: Each project should be examined to determine the most appropriate method, and an assortment of compensation methods may be used within a single project if appropriate
Mixed methods are prohibited under the SPP Documents
Only one method may ever be used per project, with no exceptions
Percentage-based fees must always be used for the entire project regardless of phase
n: Sec. 4.4.1 states that each project should be examined to determine the most appropriate and equitable method of compensation, and that using only one method may not always be applicable -- an assortment of compensation methods may be used within a single project if appropriate. (Source: Sec. 4.4.1)

q: Sec. 4.3 (Time Basis) fees are typically charged on what kind of rate?
o: A rate based solely on the final construction cost
A single fixed rate set once for the entire duration of the Architect's career
An agreed-to hourly (man-hours), daily (per diem), or monthly rate
A rate that can only be computed after project completion
n: Sec. 4.3.1 defines Time-Based Fees as fees charged on an agreed-to hourly (man-hours), daily (per diem), or per-month rate. (Source: Sec. 4.3.1)

q: Which of the following is listed under Sec. 3.2.1 as a criterion affecting the Architect's compensation?
o: The Architect's marital status
Time schedule for furnishing services and possible changes that may affect the consultant's costs
The Architect's preferred building material palette
The number of employees in the Client's own company
n: Sec. 3.2.1 lists the time schedule for furnishing services, and possible changes that may affect the consultant's costs, as a criterion to be considered in computing fees. (Source: Sec. 3.2.1 (Criteria))

q: What is the Direct Cost for the engagement above?
scenario: An Architect's office is engaged to perform non-creative, MDPE-eligible work for a Client -- research and data-gathering plus preparation of a feasibility report (no creative design work is involved). The Architect logs 40 hours at his rate of P800.00/hour; a Consultant logs 20 hours at P600.00/hour; and Technical staff log 60 hours at P350.00/hour. The parties agree on a multiplier (M) of 2.0. Reimbursable expenses (R) for the engagement total P15,000.00.

q: Which sequence correctly reflects when each type of Project Construction Cost is typically established, from earliest to latest in a project's life?
o: FPCC -> APCC -> PPCC
PPCC and FPCC are established simultaneously, followed by APCC
APCC -> PPCC -> FPCC
PPCC (at signing of Service Agreement) -> APCC (at contract award) -> FPCC (at project completion)
n: PPCC is agreed upon at the signing of the Service Agreement (Sec. 4.1.1.3.1), APCC is fixed once the winning contractor's bid is awarded (Sec. 4.1.1.3.2), and FPCC is finalized from Cost Records upon project completion (Sec. 4.1.1.3.3). (Source: Sec. 4.1.1.3.1-4.1.1.3.3)

q: Why does Sec. 4.3.8.1 state that MDPE does not account for creative design work?
o: Because the value of creative design cannot be measured by the length of time the designer has spent on the work
Because creative design always costs less than non-creative work
Because creative design work is illegal to bill on a time basis
Because creative design is compensated only through Retainer agreements
n: Sec. 4.3.8.1 explains MDPE does not account for creative work because the value of creative design cannot be measured by the length of time the designer spent on it -- unlike non-creative technical tasks. (Source: Sec. 4.3.8.1)

q: Why does Sec. 4 state that it is 'impractical to generalize any one fee basis as preferable for a specific project'?
o: Because architectural fees are affected by many variables, so compensation methods may be combined or modified as needed
Because the PRC has not yet approved any fee basis
Because only percentage-based fees are legally enforceable
Because time-basis fees are prohibited for licensed architects
n: Sec. 4 explains that architectural fees are affected by many variables, so no one fee basis can be generalized as preferable -- compensation may instead be computed using one or a combination of methods, with modifications as needed for the type of service or specific case. (Source: Sec. 4 (Methods of Compensation))

q: The Per Diem or Hourly Basis method (Sec. 4.3.12.1) is particularly suited to what kind of engagement, and what does the per diem compensate the Professional Consulting Architect (PCA) for?
o: Engagements where no travel is ever involved
Only construction-phase supervision engagements
Only full-time, continuous engagements lasting several years
Engagements involving intermittent personal service; the PCA is compensated for all time devoted to the work, including travel time
n: Sec. 4.3.12.1 states this method is particularly suited to engagements involving intermittent personal service, and that the PCA is compensated for all the time devoted to the work, including travel time. (Source: Sec. 4.3.12.1)

q: Based on the scenario above, what is the Architect's Professional Fee for full DAEDS services, computed on the PPCC?
n: PF = specified percentage x PCC = 8% x P25,000,000.00 = P2,000,000.00, computed here on the PPCC agreed at signing. (Source: Sec. 4.1.1.1, Sec. 4.1.1.3.1 (PPCC))
scenario: An Architect signs a Service Agreement for a project with a Probable Project Construction Cost (PPCC) of P25,000,000.00, and the parties agree on a Professional Fee rate of 8% of PCC for full DAEDS (architectural + basic engineering design) services.

q: What is the Professional Fee for the GFA portion of the project above?
n: PF for GFA = P1,800.00/sqm x 10,000 sqm = P18,000,000.00. (Source: Sec. 4.1.2 (Unit Cost Method, worked example))
scenario: A high-rise Office Building Project has 10,000 sqm of gross floor area (GFA) and 2,000 sqm of non-GFA space (per Rule VII and VIII of the NBCP). Based on historical data, the Average Project Construction Cost (PCC) is P30,000.00/sqm, and the agreed Professional Fee based on Percentage of PCC is 6%.

q: The Methods of Compensation and Schedule of Fees document was approved by the UAP National Executive Committee on what date, and under what resolution?
o: September 19, 2014, through UAP Execom Resolution 14-15 No. 2-14
October 15, 2014, through UAP NBD Resolution 14-15 No. 3-19
April 5, 2006, through PRBoA Resolution No. 2, Series of 2006
July 27, 2010, through PRBoA Resolution No. 3, Series of 2010
n: The Methods of Compensation and Schedule of Fees was approved by the UAP National Executive Committee through UAP Execom Resolution 14-15 No. 2-14 on September 19, 2014, and was later ratified by the UAP National Board of Directors on October 15, 2014 through UAP NBD Resolution 14-15 No. 3-19, before being forwarded to the PRC Board of Architecture for adoption. (Source: UAP-IAPOA Doc. 210, History (background))

q: For which of the following situations is Time-Basis compensation most useful, per Sec. 4.3.1-4.3.2?
o: Only for full architectural and engineering design of high-rise buildings
Only when the Client insists on a percentage-based fee instead
When services are difficult to determine in advance, or are interim in nature and often short in duration
Only for projects exceeding P100,000,000 in construction cost
n: Sec. 4.3.1-4.3.2 state Time Basis compensation is useful when services are difficult to determine in advance or are interim/short in duration -- e.g., not-well-defined services, pre-design services, partial services, additional services, expert-witness work, and specialist/consultancy services. (Source: Sec. 4.3.1-4.3.2)

q: The 'probability of contingencies that are not included in the estimates of design and construction costs' is listed as a fee criterion under which subsection?
n: Sec. 3.2.5 lists the probability of contingencies not included in the design-and-construction-cost estimates as a criterion affecting the Architect's compensation. (Source: Sec. 3.2.5 (Criteria))

q: Per Sec. 4.3.13.4, how may compensation under a retainer-fee agreement be structured, and how frequently are such fees typically arranged?
o: Only through court-ordered arbitration of the amount
Based on a fixed sum paid monthly, or some other mutually agreeable terms, with per diem or hourly rates for additional time; retainer fees are frequently on an annual basis
Always calculated as a percentage of the final project construction cost
Always as a single lump sum paid at the very end of the engagement
n: Sec. 4.3.13.4 states compensation may be based on a fixed sum paid monthly or other mutually agreeable terms, with per diem or hourly rates for additional time spent at the Client's request; retainer fees are frequently on an annual basis. (Source: Sec. 4.3.13.4)

q: The Professional Fee for the non-GFA portion is computed at what rate, and what is the resulting amount?
o: 25% of the GFA rate (P450.00/sqm) x 2,000 sqm = P900,000.00
100% of the GFA rate x 2,000 sqm = P1,800,000.00 (same rate, but this is a coincidence of the given numbers)
The full GFA rate (P1,800.00/sqm) x 2,000 sqm = P3,600,000.00
50% of the GFA rate (P900.00/sqm) x 2,000 sqm = P1,800,000.00
n: The non-GFA rate is 50% of the GFA rate: 50% x P1,800.00/sqm = P900.00/sqm; P900.00/sqm x 2,000 sqm = P1,800,000.00. (Source: Sec. 4.1.2 (Unit Cost Method, worked example))
scenario: A high-rise Office Building Project has 10,000 sqm of gross floor area (GFA) and 2,000 sqm of non-GFA space (per Rule VII and VIII of the NBCP). Based on historical data, the Average Project Construction Cost (PCC) is P30,000.00/sqm, and the agreed Professional Fee based on Percentage of PCC is 6%.

q: Sec. 4 classifies the methods of compensation for architectural services into how many main types, and what are they?
o: Two: Percentage-based Fee and Time Basis only
Five, one for each SPP document from 201 to 205
Four: Percentage-based Fee, Lump Sum, Time Basis, and Value-based Pricing as a wholly separate fourth type
Three: Percentage-based Fee, Lump Sum or Fixed Fee, and Time Basis
n: Sec. 4 states the 2010 SPP Documents identified several compensation methods generally classifiable into three main types: (a) Percentage-based Fee, (b) Lump Sum or Fixed Fee, and (c) Time Basis. Value-based Pricing is treated as a sub-method under Percentage-based Fee, not a separate main category. (Source: Sec. 4 (Methods of Compensation))

q: Which of the following is given as an example where Value-based Pricing may apply?
o: Sales in retail facilities, or leasing in housing or commercial office/residence developments
A government infrastructure project with no lease or sales component
A church or place of worship
A single-family residence with no income-generating component
n: The source text gives sales in retail facilities and leasing in housing or commercial office/residence developments as examples of metrics Value-based Pricing may be tied to. (Source: Sec. 4.1 (Value-based Pricing/Percentage of Gross Rentals))

q: What is the central purpose stated in the Rationale (Sec. 2) for setting parameters on the Architect's Guidelines on Methods of Compensation and Schedule of Fees?
o: To standardize the ranges by which a Client compensates an Architect in direct relation to the value of services the Architect provides
To eliminate time-basis compensation in favor of percentage-based fees only
To fix a single mandatory percentage fee for every architectural project nationwide
To replace RA 9266 with a new licensing framework for architects
n: Sec. 2.1 states that setting these parameters is paramount because it standardizes the ranges for which the Client will compensate the Architect in direct relation to the value of services provided -- it does not fix a single fee, replace RA 9266, or eliminate any method. (Source: Sec. 2.1 (Rationale))

q: What are the two general methods described for arriving at a lump-sum compensation for basic services?
o: (1) MDPE and (2) Salary Cost x Multiplier, applied simultaneously
(1) A per diem rate and (2) a retainer fee, used interchangeably
(1) A government-fixed rate and (2) a Client-set rate, whichever is lower

(1) A lump sum computed as an appropriate percentage of the probable project construction cost, and (2) direct development of a fixed amount by estimating individual cost elements plus a reasonable profit margin
n: Sec. 4.2.2.1-4.2.2.2 describes two methods: computing a lump sum as an appropriate percentage of the probable PCC, or directly developing a fixed amount by estimating individual cost-outline elements plus a reasonable profit margin -- these are frequently used concurrently, one checking the other. (Source: Sec. 4.2.2.1-4.2.2.3)

q: An architectural firm's total basic salaries (Direct Salary Expenses) for staff assigned to a project amount to P50,000.00. Using the Sec. 4.3.11 multiplier factor of 3.0, plus P10,000.00 in Reimbursable Expenses, what is the computed Fee under the Salary Cost x Multiplier method?
o: P125,000.00 (using a multiplier of 2.5, as in MDPE)
P150,000.00 (Reimbursable Expenses excluded)
n: Fee = Salary Cost x Multiplier + Reimbursable Expenses = (P50,000.00 x 3.0) + P10,000.00 = P150,000.00 + P10,000.00 = P160,000.00. Note the Salary-Cost-x-Multiplier method uses a multiplier of 3.0, distinct from the MDPE method's 1.5-2.5 range. (Source: Sec. 4.3.11.1-4.3.11.2)

q: If, in the same scenario, the Client later decides to separately contract the engineering consultants (converting the arrangement from full DAEDS to a DADS-type engagement for the Architect), and the DAEDS-equivalent PF at the final APCC of P27,000,000.00 (at 8%) is P2,160,000.00, what would the Architect's architectural-design-only fee be under Sec. 4.1.1.5?
o: P2,160,000.00 (unchanged, full amount)
n: Under Sec. 4.1.1.5, in a DADS-type arrangement the architectural design services constitute 60% of the corresponding DAEDS professional fee: 60% x P2,160,000.00 = P1,296,000.00. (Source: Sec. 4.1.1.5)
scenario: An Architect signs a Service Agreement for a project with a Probable Project Construction Cost (PPCC) of P25,000,000.00, and the parties agree on a Professional Fee rate of 8% of PCC for full DAEDS (architectural + basic engineering design) services.

q: Which of the following is NOT listed under Sec. 4.3.2 as a typical use case for time-based fees?
o: Serving as an expert witness
Full architectural and engineering design services for the entire project (DAEDS)
Specialist expertise or professional architectural consultancy services
Pre-design services
n: Sec. 4.3.2 lists services not well defined, pre-design services, partial services, additional services, expert-witness work, and specialist/consultancy services as typical uses for time-based fees -- full DAEDS design is instead typically compensated on a percentage-of-PCC basis. (Source: Sec. 4.3.2)

q: Under Sec. 4.3.12.3, how are sub-consultant and reimbursable direct expenses usually billed?
o: At exactly double the invoice cost, with no further explanation required
At a flat rate unrelated to actual invoice cost
At invoice cost plus an agreed service charge for handling
They are never billed to the Client under this method
n: Sec. 4.3.12.3 states sub-consultant and reimbursable direct expenses are usually billed at invoice cost plus an agreed service charge for handling. (Source: Sec. 4.3.12.3)

q: The Salary Cost x Multiplier method (Sec. 4.3.11) is based on what, multiplied by what factor, plus what additional item?
o: The Client's gross rental income, multiplied by a factor of 2.0, plus honoraria
The total project construction cost, multiplied by 6%, plus a fixed retainer
The total basic salaries (Direct Salary Expenses) of all Professional Consulting Architects and staff, multiplied by a factor of 3.0, plus reimbursable expenses
The Architect's per diem rate, multiplied by 1.5 to 2.5, plus overhead only
n: Sec. 4.3.11.1 states this method is based on the total basic salaries (Direct Salary Expenses) of all Professional Consulting Architects (PCAs) and their staff, multiplied by a factor of 3.0 as a multiplier, plus cost of certain reimbursable items classified as 'Direct Cost' or 'Reimbursable Expenses.' (Source: Sec. 4.3.11.1)

q: Including Reimbursable Expenses (R) of P15,000.00, what is the Total Cost of Service charged to the Client for the engagement above?
o: P130,000.00 (R is not added under MDPE)
P260,000.00 (R is separately multiplied by M)
n: Total Cost of Service = Fee + R = P130,000.00 + P15,000.00 = P145,000.00. (Source: Sec. 4.3.8 (MDPE Formula, applied))
scenario: An Architect's office is engaged to perform non-creative, MDPE-eligible work for a Client -- research and data-gathering plus preparation of a feasibility report (no creative design work is involved). The Architect logs 40 hours at his rate of P800.00/hour; a Consultant logs 20 hours at P600.00/hour; and Technical staff log 60 hours at P350.00/hour. The parties agree on a multiplier (M) of 2.0. Reimbursable expenses (R) for the engagement total P15,000.00.

q: Sec. 3.2.6 refers to which criterion for computing professional fees?
o: Number of third parties or agencies required to be consulted or furnished plans, specifications, reports, and similar documents
Number of years remaining on the Architect's PRC license
Number of prior projects the Client has undertaken
Number of floors in the proposed building
n: Sec. 3.2.6 lists the number of third parties or agencies required to be consulted, or furnished plans/specifications/reports/similar documents, as a fee-computation criterion. (Source: Sec. 3.2.6 (Criteria))

q: In the MDPE formula, what does 'n' represent, and what is the accepted range for the multiplier 'M'?
o: n = number of years of experience; M ranges from 0.5 to 1.0
n = number of drawings produced; M ranges from 3.0 to 5.0
n = number of site visits; M is always exactly 2.0
n = number of hours spent by the Architect, Consultants, and Technical staff; M ranges from 1.5 to 2.5
n: In the MDPE legend, n is the number of hours spent by the Architect, Consultants, and Technical staff, and M is the multiplier (to account for overhead and reasonable profit), ranging from 1.5 to 2.5 depending on office set-up and project complexity. (Source: Sec. 4.3.8 (MDPE Formula/Legend))

q: Under Sec. 3.1, choosing an appropriate method of compensation should primarily be based on what?
o: The Client's personal preference alone, regardless of service type
The type of services rendered, with the fee commensurate to the degree and scope of services
A fixed government-mandated schedule with no room for adjustment
The lowest fee any competing architect is willing to accept
n: Sec. 3.1 states that choosing an appropriate compensation method should be based on the type of services rendered, and the fee must be commensurate with the degree and scope of services rendered, reflecting the value and focusing the Client's attention on quality and performance. (Source: Sec. 3.1 (Criteria))

q: What are the three MDPE formulas, in the correct order of computation?
o: Direct Cost = (An + Cn + Tn) x R; Fee = Direct Cost + M; Total Cost of Service = Fee x R
Fee = An + Cn + Tn; Direct Cost = Fee x M; Total Cost of Service = Direct Cost + R
Direct Cost = An + Cn + Tn; Fee = Direct Cost x M; Total Cost of Service = Fee + R
Total Cost of Service = An + Cn + Tn; Fee = Total Cost of Service x M; Direct Cost = Fee + R
n: The MDPE formulas are applied in this order: Direct Cost = An + Cn + Tn (sum of Architect, Consultant, and Technical staff hourly costs); Fee = Direct Cost x M (the multiplier); and Total Cost of Service charged to Client = Fee + R (reimbursables). (Source: Sec. 4.3.8 (MDPE Formula/Legend))

q: Which of the following items is listed under Sec. 4.3.8.3 as chargeable to the Client as a reimbursable, in addition to the MDPE fee itself?
o: Cost of printing extra sets of drawings, reports, maps, and contract documents over the five (5) copies submitted to the Client
The Architect's personal life insurance premiums
Fees paid to unrelated competing architectural firms
The Client's own office rent
n: Sec. 4.3.8.3 lists reimbursable items including transportation, living/housing allowances (for foreign consultants, and for local consultants/technical staff assigned over 100 km away), and the cost of printing extra sets of drawings, reports, maps, and contract documents beyond the five (5) copies submitted to the Client, plus overseas/long-distance calls, technical/laboratory tests, licenses, fees, and taxes. (Source: Sec. 4.3.8.3)

q: Per Sec. 4.4.4, how might preparation of an architectural rendering or marketing materials be compensated, versus other services on the same project?
o: At a fixed price or lump sum, while other services on the same project could be compensated on a per diem rate or percentage of the construction cost
Only through a retainer arrangement lasting the life of the project
Always on a percentage-of-PCC basis identical to the rest of the project
Never compensated separately -- renderings are always bundled into the main design fee with no distinction
n: Sec. 4.4.4 gives the example that specific, determinate services such as preparing an architectural rendering or marketing materials could be provided at a fixed price or lump sum, while other services for the same project could be compensated on a per diem rate or percentage of the construction cost. (Source: Sec. 4.4.4)

q: Midway through construction, the winning contractor's bid (APCC) comes in at P27,000,000.00 -- higher than the original PPCC. Under the percentage-based-on-PCC method's flexible nature (Sec. 4.1.1.2), what happens to the Architect's fee?
o: The Architect's fee remains frozen forever at the original PPCC-based amount
The project is automatically converted to a Time-Basis fee
The Architect must personally absorb the cost difference with no fee adjustment
The Architect's professional fee adjusts correspondingly, since it is pegged to the applicable PCC (here, the updated APCC), without needing to amend the scope in the Service Agreement
n: Sec. 4.1.1.2 explains that because the fee is pegged to the project cost, it is flexible and adjusts correspondingly to changes in the applicable PCC (whether PPCC, APCC, or FPCC) without amending the scope of work in the Service Agreement. (Source: Sec. 4.1.1.2)
scenario: An Architect signs a Service Agreement for a project with a Probable Project Construction Cost (PPCC) of P25,000,000.00, and the parties agree on a Professional Fee rate of 8% of PCC for full DAEDS (architectural + basic engineering design) services.

q: Why does Sec. 4.2.3 recommend including a clearly stated time limit for performance of services in a lump-sum Service Agreement?
o: To prevent the Architect from ever billing for reimbursable expenses
Because lump-sum fees automatically expire after one year without a time limit clause
Because Philippine law prohibits open-ended service agreements of any kind

To provide a basis for additional compensation for extra time used on Owner-ordered changes after preliminary design documents are approved, since the fee remains fixed even if project parameters later change
n: Sec. 4.2.3 explains that while the lump-sum fee remains fixed, project parameters may change beyond the Architect's control; a time-limit clause with a provision for additional compensation for extra time on Owner-ordered changes (after preliminary design approval) protects against uncompensated scope creep. (Source: Sec. 4.2.3)

q: Under Sec. 4.3.8.1-4.3.8.2, how is the MDPE fee computed, and what is the range of the multiplier used?
o: By adding all costs of technical services (man-hours x rate), then multiplying by a multiplier ranging from 1.5 to 2.5 to cover overhead and profit
By applying a multiplier of 5.0 to 10.0 regardless of office set-up
By adding all costs of technical services and multiplying by a fixed multiplier of exactly 3.0
By dividing the total project construction cost by the multiplier
n: Sec. 4.3.8.1-4.3.8.2 state the computation adds all costs of technical services (man-hours x rate), then multiplies by a multiplier (ranging from 1.5 to 2.5, depending on office set-up, overhead, experience, and project complexity) to cover overhead and profit. (Source: Sec. 4.3.8.1-4.3.8.2)

q: Which time-basis fee type is described as frequently used where there is a continuing relationship on a series of Projects, establishing a fixed rate or lump sum over and above reimbursement for the Architect's technical time and overhead?
o: Per Diem or Hourly Basis
Retainer
Professional Fee + Expenses
MDPE
n: The Professional Fee + Expenses method is used where there is a continuing relationship on a series of Projects; it establishes an agreed fixed rate or lump sum over and above the reimbursement for the Architect's technical time and overhead, requiring agreement on the general scope of work. (Source: Sec. 4.3 (Professional Fee + Expenses))

q: For what kind of project is the Salary Cost x Multiplier method (Sec. 4.3.11.3) said to be best suited?
o: Projects where the Client insists on a single fixed price with no adjustment
Projects for which costs are difficult to predetermine, or which may require additional experimental or investigative work that could further alter the project's scope
Projects requiring only non-creative technical work such as data entry
Projects with a clearly and fully definable scope from the outset
n: Sec. 4.3.11.3 states this method of remuneration is best suited for projects where costs are difficult to predetermine, or where additional experimental or investigative work may become necessary, potentially altering the scope of the project. (Source: Sec. 4.3.11.3)

q: What does DADS stand for, and how does it differ from DAEDS?
o: Detailed Architectural Design Services -- identical in scope to DAEDS but billed at a higher percentage
Detailed Architect Delivery Services -- covers construction supervision only, with no design component
Detailed Architectural Design Services -- a separate contract excluding all engineering and engineering-specialist-consultant fees, with the Architect still serving as lead/prime professional
Direct Architectural Design Standard -- a government-mandated minimum design specification
n: Sec. 4.1.1.5 defines DADS (Detailed Architectural Design Services) as a separate contract from architectural services that excludes engineering and engineering-specialist-consultant fees; the Architect remains the lead/prime professional, coordinating the work of other engineering design service providers. (Source: Sec. 4.1.1.5)

q: Sec. 3.2.2 identifies which of the following as a criterion for computing professional fees?
o: The Architect's personal investment portfolio
The brand of software used to prepare the drawings
The distance between the project site and the nearest airport
Studies, programs, and other professional input furnished by the Owner or Client
n: Sec. 3.2.2 lists studies, programs, and other professional input furnished by the Owner or Client as a fee-computation criterion. (Source: Sec. 3.2.2 (Criteria))

q: Using a multiplier (M) of 2.0, what is the resulting Fee for the engagement above?
o: P130,000.00 (Direct Cost of P65,000.00 x M of 2.0)
n: Fee = Direct Cost x M = P65,000.00 x 2.0 = P130,000.00. (Source: Sec. 4.3.8 (MDPE Formula, applied))
scenario: An Architect's office is engaged to perform non-creative, MDPE-eligible work for a Client -- research and data-gathering plus preparation of a feasibility report (no creative design work is involved). The Architect logs 40 hours at his rate of P800.00/hour; a Consultant logs 20 hours at P600.00/hour; and Technical staff log 60 hours at P350.00/hour. The parties agree on a multiplier (M) of 2.0. Reimbursable expenses (R) for the engagement total P15,000.00.

q: Which criterion under Sec. 3.2.3 concerns the Client's own conduct during the project?
o: The Client's preferred bank for payment transfers
Client's procedure and timing for review and approval of the Architect's recommendations/designs
The Client's choice of interior decorator
The Client's nationality
n: Sec. 3.2.3 lists the Client's procedure and timing for review and approval of the Architect's recommendations/designs as a criterion affecting fee computation. (Source: Sec. 3.2.3 (Criteria))

q: Using the Unit Cost Method, what is the computed Professional Fee per square meter for the project above?
n: PF per sqm = PCC per sqm x rate = P30,000.00 x 0.06 = P1,800.00/sqm. (Source: Sec. 4.1.2 (Unit Cost Method, worked example))
scenario: A high-rise Office Building Project has 10,000 sqm of gross floor area (GFA) and 2,000 sqm of non-GFA space (per Rule VII and VIII of the NBCP). Based on historical data, the Average Project Construction Cost (PCC) is P30,000.00/sqm, and the agreed Professional Fee based on Percentage of PCC is 6%.

q: Under Sec. 4.1.1.5, when architectural services are contracted separately from engineering services (DADS arrangement), what portion of the stated Professional Fee (PF) for DAEDS do the architectural design services constitute?
o: One hundred percent (100%)
Sixty percent (60%)
Seventy-five percent (75%)
Fifty percent (50%)
n: Sec. 4.1.1.5 states the architectural design services shall constitute sixty percent (60%) of the corresponding stated professional fee (PF) for DAEDS for the project. (Source: Sec. 4.1.1.5)

q: What is the formula used to compute the fee under the Salary Cost x Multiplier method?
o: Fee = Reimbursable Expenses x Multiplier - Salary Cost
Fee = Salary Cost / Multiplier + Reimbursable Expenses
Fee = Direct Cost x Multiplier (same as the MDPE formula, with no separate reimbursable term)
Fee = Salary Cost (Direct Salary Expenses) x Multiplier + Reimbursable Expenses
n: Sec. 4.3.11.2 gives the formula: Fee = Salary Cost (or Direct Salary Expenses) x Multiplier + Reimbursable Expenses. (Source: Sec. 4.3.11.2)

q: What additional function does the chosen method of compensation serve for the Client, according to Sec. 3.1?
o: It automatically waives the Client's right to review the Architect's designs
It legally binds the Client to use the same Architect on all future projects
It determines the Client's construction loan interest rate
It serves as a basis for the Client to pre-determine his costs for architectural services
n: Sec. 3.1 states the method of compensation will serve as a basis for the Client to pre-determine his costs for architectural services. (Source: Sec. 3.1 (Criteria))

q: Under Sec. 4.1.1, what is described as the most common method of compensation for architectural services worldwide?
o: Retainer
Per Diem or Hourly Basis
Percentage based on Project Construction Cost (PCC)
Multiple of Direct Personnel Expense (MDPE)
n: Sec. 4.1.1.1 states that percentage-based compensation on Project Construction Cost is the most common method of compensation for architectural services worldwide. (Source: Sec. 4.1.1.1)

q: Per Sec. 3.2, how should compensation for services requiring more than one type of expertise be treated relative to services requiring only one (or related) type of expertise?
o: They shall always be treated identically, using the same percentage
They shall be treated differently
Multi-expertise services shall always be billed at a lower rate
The distinction is irrelevant to how fees are computed
n: Sec. 3.2 states that compensation for services requiring only one kind of expertise (or related types) shall be treated differently from those requiring more than one type of expertise, since fee computation depends on the complexity and types of services involved. (Source: Sec. 3.2 (Criteria))

q: Per Sec. 4.4.3, when dealing with authorities having jurisdiction and obtaining project approvals (a task of indeterminate complexity and time), what compensation approach is suggested, versus the compensation for project documentation itself?
o: A single lump-sum fee covering both tasks equally, with no distinction
An agreed-to hourly rate for dealing with authorities/approvals, while project documentation is compensated on a percentage fee based on construction cost
Value-based pricing tied to the Client's eventual building occupancy rate for both tasks
A retainer fee for both tasks, renewable annually
n: Sec. 4.4.3 gives the example that because dealing with authorities and obtaining approvals can be indeterminate in complexity and time, it may be fair to compensate the Architect on an agreed-to hourly rate for that task, while the project documentation itself could be compensated on a percentage fee based on the construction cost. (Source: Sec. 4.4.3)

q: Which resolution and date mark the PRC's approval of the (updated) Standards of Professional Practice (SPP), ahead of which the Methods of Compensation and Schedule of Fees document was later added?
o: PRBoA Resolution No. 2, Series of 2006, April 5, 2006
UAP NBD Resolution 14-15 No. 3-19, October 15, 2014
PRBoA Resolution No. 3, Series of 2010, July 27, 2010
UAP Execom Resolution 14-15 No. 2-14, September 19, 2014
n: The New/Updated SPP was approved by the PRC through PRBoA Resolution No. 3, Series of 2010, on July 27, 2010 -- ahead of the Methods of Compensation and Schedule of Fees document being added to complete the SPP Docs. (Source: UAP-IAPOA Doc. 210, History (background))

q: How is the Architect's Professional Fee (PF) determined under the Percentage-based-on-PCC method?
o: By adding the Architect's daily rate to a fixed lump sum
By dividing the total construction cost by the number of years of design work
By multiplying the specified percentage by the estimated, awarded, or final Project Construction Cost (PCC)
By multiplying the gross floor area by the Architect's hourly rate
n: Sec. 4.1.1.1 states the PF is determined by multiplying the specified percentage by the estimated, awarded, or final Project Construction Cost (PCC) of the project. (Source: Sec. 4.1.1.1)

q: According to Sec. 4.3.6, when should additional (overtime) factors be considered in time-basis billing?
o: When overtime work is undertaken at the Client's request or to meet scheduling demands beyond the Architect's control
Never -- overtime cannot be billed under any time-basis method
Only when the Architect personally decides to work extra hours for no reason
Only on national holidays
n: Sec. 4.3.6 states additional factors for overtime expenses should be considered if such work is undertaken at the Client's request or to meet scheduling demands beyond the Architect's control. (Source: Sec. 4.3.6)

q: What does 'R' represent in the MDPE formula, and in which final equation does it appear?
o: R = Retainer fee; it appears in Direct Cost = An + Cn + Tn + R
R = Reimbursable expenses (e.g., transportation, housing, living allowances); it appears in Total Cost of Service = Fee + R
R = Renovation surcharge; it replaces the multiplier M entirely
R = Rate of return on investment; it does not appear in any MDPE equation
n: R stands for Reimbursable expenses (such as transportation, housing, and living allowances of Consultants and staff), and it is added to the Fee in the final equation: Total Cost of Service charged to Client = Fee + R. (Source: Sec. 4.3.8 (MDPE Formula/Legend))

q: For Building Administration and Management Services, when may an Architect's remuneration be based on a certain percentage of gross rentals?
o: Only when the building is government-owned
When the Architect goes beyond maintenance and upkeep functions by innovating schemes to attain maximum building occupancy and efficient/economical operation
Whenever the Architect is merely asked to change lightbulbs and perform routine repairs
Never -- percentage of gross rentals is exclusive to Percentage-based-on-PCC fees
n: The source specifies that when the Architect employed by the Client goes beyond maintenance/upkeep by innovating schemes for maximum occupancy and efficient/economical operation of a building, facility, or complex, remuneration may be based on a percentage of gross rentals. (Source: Sec. 4.1 (Value-based Pricing/Percentage of Gross Rentals))

q: Per Sec. 3 (Criteria), the criteria for computing the Architect's compensation should be based on a mutual evaluation of which factors?
o: The Architect's/firm's talents, skill, experience, effort, and time available for and required by the project
Only the prevailing market interest rate at the time of contract signing
Only the number of years the Architect has been licensed
Only the total square meterage of the project
n: Sec. 3 states the criteria for computing compensation should be based on mutual evaluation of the Architect's/firm's talents, skill, experience, effort, and time available for, and required by, the project. (Source: Sec. 3 (Criteria))

q: A 'mutually agreed-upon Probable Project Construction Cost' using unit price parameters (prevailing market construction cost per sqm) established on the date of signing of the Service Agreement is known as which type of PCC?
o: GFA (Gross Floor Area) Cost
FPCC (Final Project Construction Cost)
APCC (Awarded Project Construction Cost)
PPCC (Probable Project Construction Cost)
n: Sec. 4.1.1.3.1 defines the PPCC as the mutually agreed-upon Probable Project Construction Cost, using unit price parameters established on the date the Service Agreement is signed. (Source: Sec. 4.1.1.3.1)

q: Under the Per Diem, Honorarium plus Reimbursable Expenses method (Sec. 4.3.10), which of the following activities may require the Architect's personal time and be compensated this way?
o: Filing the Architect's own income tax return
Attending project-related meetings, conferences, or trips; conducting ocular inspection of possible project sites; and conferring with others regarding prospective investments or ventures
Preparing the final as-built drawing set
Supervising the pouring of structural concrete
n: Sec. 4.3.10 lists attending project-related meetings/conferences/trips, conducting ocular inspection of possible project sites, and conferring with others regarding prospective investments or ventures as activities that may be compensated on a per diem and honorarium basis. (Source: Sec. 4.3.10)

q: What is the Unit Cost Method, as described under Sec. 4.1.2?
o: A flat government-set rate per project regardless of size
A method that ignores construction cost entirely in favor of the Architect's personal hourly rate
A method used only for renovation work, never for new construction
A variation of the percentage-based-on-PCC method, where remuneration is based on cost per square meter (or other unit) of the project, requiring accurate and timely cost data
n: Sec. 4.1.2 describes the Unit Cost Method as a variation of the percentage-based-on-PCC method, where the Professional Fee is based on a computed unit cost parameter (cost per sqm or other unit such as room or store), requiring accurate and timely data on the cost of providing services for each unit. (Source: Sec. 4.1.2)

q: Before a lump-sum fee can be set under Sec. 4.2.1, what must the Client and Architect agree on?
o: The Client's choice of general contractor exclusively
The details of the scope of the project, schedules for design and approvals, construction schedules, and other variables defining the extent of services
Only the Architect's personal daily rate
Only the total construction cost, with no need to define scope
n: Sec. 4.2.1 requires the Client and Architect to agree on the scope of the project, schedules for design and approvals, construction schedules, and other variables so the Architect can prepare a comprehensive estimate of work hours and overhead costs. (Source: Sec. 4.2.1)

q: The Code of Ethical Conduct (SPP Doc. 200) was approved through which resolution?
o: UAP NBD Resolution 14-15 No. 3-19 (October 15, 2014)
PRBoA Resolution No. 2, Series of 2006 (April 5, 2006)
PRBoA Resolution No. 3, Series of 2010 (July 27, 2010)
UAP Execom Resolution 14-15 No. 2-14 (September 19, 2014)
n: The Code of Ethical Conduct was approved on April 5, 2006 through PRBoA Resolution No. 2, Series of 2006. (Source: UAP-IAPOA Doc. 210, History (background))

q: What factors does Sec. 4.3.13.3 say the amount of a retainer fee varies with?
o: The character and value of the services to the Client, and the reputation and standing of the consultant in the profession
The Client's annual revenue exclusively
Only the total floor area of all projects covered
A fixed government schedule with no room for variation
n: Sec. 4.3.13.3 states the amount of the retainer varies with the character and value of the services to the Client, and the reputation and standing of the consultant in his or her profession. (Source: Sec. 4.3.13.3)

q: When is the Lump Sum or Fixed Fee method of compensation (Sec. 4.2) most appropriately used?
o: When the scope of services is expected to change frequently and unpredictably
Only for Pre-Design Services
Only when the Client refuses to disclose the project budget
When the scope of services required can be clearly and fully defined at the outset of the project
n: Sec. 4.2.1 states this method may be used when the scope of services required can be clearly and fully defined at the outset of the project. (Source: Sec. 4.2.1)

q: What is the Total Professional Fee for DAEDS Services for the project above?
o: P18,000,000.00 (GFA only, non-GFA is not compensated)
n: Total DAEDS PF = PF for GFA + PF for non-GFA = P18,000,000.00 + P1,800,000.00 = P19,800,000.00. (Source: Sec. 4.1.2 (Unit Cost Method, worked example))
scenario: A high-rise Office Building Project has 10,000 sqm of gross floor area (GFA) and 2,000 sqm of non-GFA space (per Rule VII and VIII of the NBCP). Based on historical data, the Average Project Construction Cost (PCC) is P30,000.00/sqm, and the agreed Professional Fee based on Percentage of PCC is 6%.

q: According to Sec. 2 (Rationale), the Architect's Guidelines on Methods of Compensation are meant to complement which of the following?
o: Local government building-permit ordinances exclusively
RA 9266 (The Architecture Act of 2004), the Code of Ethical Conduct, and the Standards of Professional Practice (SPP Docs. 201-209)
Only the Civil Code provisions on contracts
Only the National Building Code of the Philippines (NBCP)
n: Sec. 2.1 states the Guidelines complement the existing professional regulatory law (RA 9266), the Architect's National Code (i.e., the Code of Ethical Conduct, SPP Doc. 200) and the Standards of Professional Practice (SPP Docs. 201-209), and other related PRC-approved rules -- nothing in the Guidelines should unduly affect those laws/policies. (Source: Sec. 2.1 (Rationale))

q: An Architect and Client agree that the full DAEDS professional fee for a project (architectural + basic structural/plumbing/sanitary/mechanical/electrical engineering design) would be P4,000,000 if contracted as a single package. If instead the Client hires the engineering consultants separately (a DADS arrangement) and the Architect only provides architectural design services while coordinating the engineers, how much should the Architect's architectural design fee be under Sec. 4.1.1.5?
o: P4,000,000 (the full DAEDS PF)
P1,000,000 (25% of the DAEDS PF)
P2,000,000 (50% of the DAEDS PF)
n: Sec. 4.1.1.5 provides that in a DADS-type arrangement, the architectural design services constitute 60% of the corresponding DAEDS professional fee: 60% x P4,000,000 = P2,400,000. (Source: Sec. 4.1.1.5)

q: Value-based Pricing (Percentage of Gross Rentals), as described under Percentage-based Fee, computes remuneration based on what?
o: The Architect's hourly billing rate multiplied by 2.5
A fixed government schedule unrelated to the project's financial performance
The total floor area only, without reference to any financial outcome
The outcome, revenue, cost, and profitability results of the project engagement, or a measurable profit on specific Client revenues
n: Under Value-based Pricing, remuneration is based on the outcome of revenue, cost, and profitability results of the project engagement, or a measurable profit on specific revenues to the Client. (Source: Sec. 4.1 (Value-based Pricing/Percentage of Gross Rentals))

q: According to Sec. 4.1.2, why does renovation work typically require a different (often higher) service effort under the Unit Cost Method than a comparable new unit?
o: Because renovation work is legally classified as a separate profession
Because renovation is always billed at exactly half the rate of new construction
Because renovation of a unit requires more service effort than a new unit
Because the Unit Cost Method cannot legally be applied to renovation projects
n: Sec. 4.1.2 explicitly notes that unit cost estimation requires accurate and timely data, and that renovation of a unit requires more service effort than a new unit of the same type. (Source: Sec. 4.1.2)

q: An Architect's office is located in Metro Manila. A project site is 150 kilometers away (air/straight-line/radial distance) from the Architect's established office as it appears on the Architect's letterhead. Under the SPP Doc. 202 travel-time rule referenced in Sec. 4.3, is a per diem plus traveling and living expenses chargeable to the Owner?
o: Only if the Architect travels by airplane rather than by car
Yes -- because the distance exceeds 100.0 km (air/straight-line/radial distance) from the Architect's established office
Only if the site is outside the Philippines
No -- travel expenses are never chargeable regardless of distance
n: SPP Doc. 202 provides that a per diem plus traveling and living expenses shall be chargeable to the Owner whenever the Architect (or authorized representative) is required to perform services at a locality beyond 100.0 km (air, straight line, or radial distance) from the established office as shown on the Architect's letterhead. At 150 km, this threshold is exceeded. (Source: SPP Doc. 202, cited in Sec. 4.3 (Time Basis))

q: Sec. 4.4.2 gives an example of mixed compensation methods involving which two service phases and their respective fee bases?
o: Pre-Design Services and Construction Services compensated on MDPE, while Regular and Specialized Allied Design Services are paid on a Percentage of Project Construction Cost basis
All phases compensated on a single Lump-Sum fee with no variation
Pre-Design Services compensated on Retainer, while all other services are compensated on Value-based Pricing exclusively
Construction Services compensated on Percentage of PCC, while Pre-Design Services are compensated on Retainer only
n: Sec. 4.4.2 gives the example that Pre-Design Services and Construction Services could be compensated on a Multiple of Direct Personnel Expense basis, while the Regular and Specialized Allied Design Services could be paid on a Percentage of Project Construction Cost (or Percentage of Cost of Work) basis. (Source: Sec. 4.4.2)

q: Sec. 4.3.8.1 states the Multiple of Direct Personnel Expenses (MDPE) method is applicable only to which kind of work?
o: Any type of architectural work without restriction
Non-creative work, such as accounting, secretarial work, research, data gathering, and preparation of reports
Construction supervision exclusively
Creative design work exclusively
n: Sec. 4.3.8.1 states MDPE is a cost-based method applicable only to non-creative work such as accounting, secretarial work, research, data gathering, and preparation of reports, since it is based on technical hours spent. (Source: Sec. 4.3.8.1)

q: Would MDPE be an appropriate compensation method if the same office's staff instead spent those hours producing creative conceptual design schemes for the Client's building?
o: Yes, but only if the multiplier is raised above 2.5
No -- per Sec. 4.3.8.1, MDPE applies only to non-creative work, since the value of creative design cannot be measured by time spent
Yes -- MDPE applies equally well to creative and non-creative work
No -- MDPE is reserved exclusively for construction supervision work
n: Sec. 4.3.8.1 restricts MDPE to non-creative work such as accounting, secretarial work, research, data gathering, and report preparation -- creative design work cannot be fairly measured by technical hours spent, so a different method (e.g., percentage-based or lump-sum) is more appropriate. (Source: Sec. 4.3.8.1)
scenario: An Architect's office is engaged to perform non-creative, MDPE-eligible work for a Client -- research and data-gathering plus preparation of a feasibility report (no creative design work is involved). The Architect logs 40 hours at his rate of P800.00/hour; a Consultant logs 20 hours at P600.00/hour; and Technical staff log 60 hours at P350.00/hour. The parties agree on a multiplier (M) of 2.0. Reimbursable expenses (R) for the engagement total P15,000.00.

q: Under Sec. 4.3.10.2, in addition to a per diem and honorarium, what else may the Architect (as agent of the Owner) be paid for these particular activities?
o: Nothing further -- the honorarium is the sole and complete compensation
A percentage of the Owner's eventual investment returns
A fixed annual salary regardless of hours spent
Out-of-pocket expenses such as, but not limited to, travel, accommodations, and subsistence
n: Sec. 4.3.10.2 states the Architect may be paid on a per diem and honorarium basis plus out-of-pocket expenses such as, but not limited to, travel, accommodations, and subsistence. (Source: Sec. 4.3.10.2)

q: What factors does Sec. 4.1.1.1 say the applicable percentage varies with?
o: Only whether the Client is a private individual or a government agency
Classification of building, complexity of building requirements, construction value, type of construction contract, and other adjustment factors
Only the Architect's number of years in practice
Only the region where the Architect's office is registered
n: Sec. 4.1.1.1 states the percentage varies depending on building classification, complexity of building requirements, construction value, type of construction contract, and other adjustment factors constituting the extent of the Architect's work. (Source: Sec. 4.1.1.1)

q: What document does UAP-IAPOA Doc. 210 (Architect's Guidelines for Standards of Professional Practice Compliances - Methods of Compensation and Schedule of Fees) replace?
o: The 1979 UAP Doc. 208-B (Methods of Compensation and Schedule of Fees)
SPP Doc. 200 (Code of Ethical Conduct)
RA 9266 (The Architecture Act of 2004)
The 2010 SPP Documents in their entirety
n: The title clause of Doc. 210 states it replaces the 1979 UAP Doc. 208-B, which previously covered Methods of Compensation and Schedule of Fees. (Source: UAP-IAPOA Doc. 210, Sec. 1 (Title))

q: Using the same 100-km travel-time rule, if a project site is only 80 kilometers (air/straight-line/radial distance) from the Architect's established office, what is the rule's effect on chargeable per diem and travel/living expenses?
o: The rule still automatically applies because 80 km is close to 100 km
The 100-km-threshold rule for automatically chargeable per diem/travel expenses does not apply, since 80 km does not exceed 100.0 km
The Architect must refund any travel costs already incurred
The project is automatically reclassified as a Lump-Sum engagement
n: SPP Doc. 202's rule triggers automatic chargeability of per diem plus traveling/living expenses only beyond 100.0 km (air/straight-line/radial distance) from the Architect's established office. At 80 km, that specific threshold is not met. (Source: SPP Doc. 202, cited in Sec. 4.3 (Time Basis))

q: Why is percentage-based-on-PCC compensation described as fair to both Client and Architect, and flexible?
o: Because it guarantees the Architect a fixed minimum income regardless of project size
Because the fee is pegged to the project cost, and adjusts automatically with changes/additions/deductions without amending the scope in the Service Agreement
Because it eliminates the need for the Architect to track construction costs at all
Because it is the only method that requires no written agreement
n: Sec. 4.1.1.2 explains the fee is pegged to the cost of the project the Client is willing to undertake, so it is fair to both parties and adjusts easily to changes, additions, or deductions in the work without needing to amend the Service Agreement's scope. (Source: Sec. 4.1.1.2)

q: Sec. 3.2.4 lists which item as a criterion in computing the Architect's professional fee?
o: The Client's annual gross income
The cost of the Architect's personal vehicle
Fees charged by unrelated third-party real-estate brokers
Costs of administration, including records to be maintained and preserved
n: Sec. 3.2.4 lists costs of administration, including records to be maintained and preserved, as a relevant fee-computation criterion. (Source: Sec. 3.2.4 (Criteria))

q: Before agreeing to use the MDPE method, what must the Architect disclose to the Client at the start of the commission, per Sec. 4.3.8.3?
o: The Architect's personal home address
The professionals and personnel who will be assigned to the Project, and the multiplier that will be applied
The exact retail price of every material to be specified
The names of all competing bidders for the project
n: Sec. 4.3.8.3 requires that, at the start of the commission, the Architect make known the professionals and personnel who will be assigned to the Project and the multiplier to be applied, before agreeing on this method of compensation. (Source: Sec. 4.3.8.3)

q: What does DAEDS stand for, and what does it typically include?
o: Design and Engineering Development Services -- structural engineering design only
Direct Architectural Expense Design Services -- reimbursable expenses only
Detailed Architectural and Engineering Design Services -- the architectural design plus normal basic structural, plumbing, sanitary, mechanical, and electrical engineering design services
Detailed Architectural and Estimation Design Services -- architectural design plus quantity surveying only
n: Sec. 4.1.1.4 defines DAEDS (Detailed Architectural and Engineering Design Services) as the most common contract type, comprising architectural design plus the normal basic engineering design services for structural, plumbing, sanitary, mechanical, and electrical systems -- desirable when the Client wants single-point responsibility for the Project Design. (Source: Sec. 4.1.1.4)

q: When a lump-sum fee must be equitably adjusted due to changed conditions, on what basis is the adjustment usually determined?
o: The Architect's original bid price only, without any additional computation
A cost-plus basis considering estimated drawings, staff hours and salaries, schedule requirements, overhead costs, reimbursable expenses, and reasonable profit
A simple percentage increase equal to inflation with no other factors considered
Arbitration by the PRC Board of Architecture in every instance
n: Sec. 4.2.3 states fee adjustments are usually determined on a cost-plus basis, considering the estimated number of drawings, staff hours and salaries, schedule requirements, overhead costs, reimbursable expenses, and reasonable profit needed to complete the additional services. (Source: Sec. 4.2.3)

q: Sec. 4.3.7 recommends that the Client and Architect agree, at the outset, on which additional matter besides the hourly/per-diem rates themselves?
o: The Client's future hiring of additional in-house architects
A permanent, unchangeable rate that can never be revisited
A rate that automatically doubles every five years
A time period for review and adjustment of the hourly rates (e.g., annually), to account for inflation and other factors
n: Sec. 4.3.7 states the Client and Architect should agree upon a time period (perhaps annually) for review and adjustment of the hourly rates, in order to adjust for inflation and other factors. (Source: Sec. 4.3.7)

q: The Retainer method (Sec. 4.3.13.1) is used under what circumstance, and what does the Client receive in exchange for the stipulated periodic payment?
o: Used exclusively for expert-witness court testimony
Used to guarantee the Architect a percentage of gross rentals

Used when the PCA's services are expected to be required at intervals over time; the Client is assured in advance that the PCA's services will be available when required, obligating the PCA to render certain services or spend certain time on the Client's requirements
Used only for one-time, single-visit engagements
n: Sec. 4.3.13.1 explains the Retainer method is used when a PCA's services are expected to be needed at intervals over a period of time, ensuring in advance that the PCA's services will be available; a stipulated amount is paid at regular intervals in exchange for the PCA rendering certain services or spending a certain amount of time on the Client's requirements, with the minimum services covered and additional services paid separately. (Source: Sec. 4.3.13.1)

q: Sec. 4.3.5 identifies two types of fee multipliers used in hourly billing. Which one is described as the most common?
o: Gross Rental Percentage
Direct Salary Expenses
Direct Personnel Expenses
Final Project Construction Cost
n: Sec. 4.3.5 states there are two types of multipliers -- one of Direct Salary Expenses and another of Direct Personnel Expenses -- and that Direct Personnel Expenses is the most common. (Source: Sec. 4.3.5)

q: Which type of Project Construction Cost is based on the bid of the winning contractor?
o: FPCC (Final Project Construction Cost)
PPCC (Probable Project Construction Cost)
APCC (Awarded Project Construction Cost)
DAEDS Cost
n: Sec. 4.1.1.3.2 defines APCC as the Awarded Project Construction Cost, based on the bid of the winning contractor. (Source: Sec. 4.1.1.3.2)

q: Which type of Project Construction Cost is based on Cost Records submitted to the Architect upon completion of the project, including payments to the contractor, sub-contractors, and owner-supplied materials?
o: APCC (Awarded Project Construction Cost)
FPCC (Final Project Construction Cost)
PPCC (Probable Project Construction Cost)
Unit Cost Parameter
n: Sec. 4.1.1.3.3 defines FPCC as the Final Project Construction Cost, based on Cost Records submitted upon project completion, covering all payments to the contractor and sub-contractors, cost of owner-supplied materials, and other acquisitions constituting the actual total construction cost of elements designed or specified by the Architect. (Source: Sec. 4.1.1.3.3)

q: In the MDPE formula legend, what do the variables A, C, and T represent, respectively?
o: A = Awarded PCC, C = Cost-plus basis, T = Time-basis multiplier
A = Area, C = Construction cost, T = Time limit
A = Architect's rate/hour, C = Consultant's rate/hour, T = Technical Staff's rate/hour
A = Approval date, C = Client's budget, T = Total fee
n: The MDPE formula legend defines A as the Architect's rate per hour, C as the Consultant's rate per hour, and T as the rate per hour of Technical Staff, Inspectors, and others involved in the Project. (Source: Sec. 4.3.8 (MDPE Formula/Legend))

q: Per Sec. 4.3.12.2, hourly fees under this method are especially well suited for which kind of work?
o: Full architectural and engineering design of an entire high-rise project
Percentage-of-PCC billing on the final construction cost
Long-term retainer engagements exclusively
Consultation services, testimony in court, or similar work involving miscellaneous personal service
n: Sec. 4.3.12.2 states hourly fees are well suited for consultation services, testimony in court, or similar work involving miscellaneous personal service, and that most Architects have standard published schedules of hourly rates for various classifications of employees. (Source: Sec. 4.3.12.2)
